summary: Describes how to carry alarm information inside syslog messages. It maps the ITU perceived-severity levels onto syslog message fields and defines structured-data parameters taken from X.733 and the IETF Alarm MIB. This is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A building has fire alarms that range from small warnings to big emergencies. This document gives computers a shared way to write those alarm levels into their log messages so every tool understands how serious each one is.

questions: how to send alarms in syslog
how do itu severities map to syslog
what is the alarm sd-id in syslog
how do itu severities map to syslog severity
subtitle: How to carry alarm details in syslog messages and map ITU alarm severities onto syslog severities.

tldr.problem: Many implementations log alarms through syslog as well as through SNMP or Netconf, but syslog has its own severity values and no standard place for alarm fields.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a mapping from ITU perceived severities to syslog SEVERITY, and an "alarm" structured-data element with parameters such as resource, probableCause and perceivedSeverity.
tldr.outcome: Alarm logs can carry the unmodified ITU severity and the same resource and cause names used in the Alarm MIB, so they are easier to correlate with alarms from other protocols.

today: RFC 5674 is a Proposed Standard from October 2009. It is not marked as obsoleted or updated in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Alarms Go Into Syslog
sections.content:
Alarm information is often sent asynchronously through protocols such as SNMP or the Network Configuration Protocol (Netconf). The RFC notes that many implementations also log alarms through syslog. This memo defines a set of SD-PARAMs to support that logging, plus a mapping from alarm severity to syslog severity.

The terms and fields come from the Alarm MIB in RFC 3877, which includes the mandatory alarm fields from ITU-T X.733 and information from X.736. Syslog terms such as SD-ID and SD-PARAM are defined in RFC 5424.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers already have a way to shout about problems. This document lets them write the shout into the same diary they use for everything else, in a way every reader understands.

sections.title: Severity Mapping
sections.content:
The Alarm MIB defines ITU perceived severities. Syslog has its own SEVERITY values, defined in RFC 5424, and the two sets do not line up one to one. The RFC says the mapping in its Table 1 SHOULD be used.

Because the mapping loses information (for example, both Indeterminate and Cleared map to Notice), the RFC also defines a structured-data element that carries the unmodified ITU perceived severity.

Syslog severity 5 (Notice) is used for both Indeterminate and Cleared, so the syslog severity alone cannot tell them apart.
sections.plainLanguage: Alarm levels and log levels are like two different rulers. They do not match perfectly, so the exact alarm level is also written down separately.

sections.title: The alarm Structured Data Element
sections.content:
Syslog STRUCTURED-DATA allows structured information to be placed in a message. This RFC defines an alarm SD-ID to hold alarm data. Supporting it is optional, but once it is supported, some of its SD-PARAMs are mandatory.

  • resource (MUST): uniquely identifies the resource under alarm within the scope of a network element.
  • probableCause (MUST): the mnemonic of the IANAItuProbableCause object from RFC 3877, for example transmissionError.
  • perceivedSeverity (MUST): one of cleared, indeterminate, critical, major, minor or warning.
  • eventType (SHOULD): the mnemonic of the IANAItuEventType object, for example environmentalAlarm.
  • trendIndication (SHOULD): moreSevere, noChange or lessSevere.
  • resourceURI (SHOULD): a URI identifying the resource under alarm.

The resourceURI value MUST conform to the URI definition in RFC 3986. For an SNMP resource, the syntax in RFC 4088 MUST be used, and the URI must point to the same resource as alarmActiveResourceId for that alarm. This makes it easy to correlate the syslog alarm with alarms received through other protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Each alarm note has a few labeled boxes: what broke, why it probably broke, and how bad it is. Some boxes must be filled in and some are nice to have.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The first example extends a message from RFC 5424. It has two structured-data elements: the original example element and a new alarm element holding the three mandatory parameters, resource, probableCause and perceivedSeverity. The message has VERSION 1, Facility 4 and severity 2, and the BOM at the start of the MSG indicates UTF-8.

The second example adds two optional parameters, eventType and resourceURI. Here the resource is interface 42 and the URI is an snmp:// URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a finished alarm note: first with only the required boxes filled in, then with a couple of extra ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond the general syslog considerations in RFC 5424, alarms may tell an attacker which parts of a system are currently under stress, and give general information such as inventory.

Users should not have access to information in alarms that their normal access permissions would not permit through another route. The RFC adds that syslog has no standardized access control model, so filtering alarms by receiver identity is at best implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: An alarm log shows where a building is weak, so only the right people should be allowed to read it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the alarm syslog Structured Data ID and its PARAM-NAMEs. The registry marks resource, probableCause and perceivedSeverity as MANDATORY, and eventType, trendIndication and resourceURI as OPTIONAL.
sections.plainLanguage: The names of the boxes were written in an official list so nobody else reuses them for something different.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE 2 FROM THE RFC, WRAPPED FOR READING

data.title: Alarm with optional parameters
data.code:
<165>1 2004-11-10T20:15:15.003Z mymachine.example.com
evntslog - ID48 [alarm resource="interface 42"
probableCause="unauthorizedAccessAttempt"
perceivedSeverity="major"
eventType="communicationsAlarm"
resourceURI="snmp://example.com//1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.1.42"]
